extracted.subtask_description: A detailed punctuation style guide specifying rules for periods, commas, colons, semicolons, quotation marks, dashes, parentheses, brackets, ellipses, hyphens, and related matters aimed at standardizing punctuation in published texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 124. Use no period after Roman numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not place a period after Roman numerals, even if they have the value of ordinals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. IV; Louis XVI was on the throne.

rubrics_metrics.name: 125. Omit period after running-heads and certain headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the period after running-heads, centered headlines, side-heads set in separate lines, cut-in heads, box-heads in tables, superscriptions and legends that do not form a complete sentence, date lines at top of communications, and signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These items lack a terminal period when they don't form a complete sentence (see cross-reference to rule 50).

rubrics_metrics.name: 126. Period placement with quotation marks and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the period inside the quotation marks; place it inside parentheses when the enclosed matter is an independent sentence and forms no part of the preceding sentence; otherwise place it outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as a rule without exception. Examples: Tennyson's "In Memoriam." ; When the parentheses form part of the preceding sentence, put the period outside.

rubrics_metrics.name: 127. Use of the exclamation point
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the exclamation point to mark an outcry, or an emphatic or ironical utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "Long live the king!" "Heaven forbid!" "Good!". Also used sometimes for ironic or emphatic parenthetical remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: 128. Exclamation point placement relative to quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the exclamation point inside the quotation marks when it is part of the quotation; otherwise outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See illustrations in rule 127 for usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: 129. Use of the interrogation point (question mark)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the interrogation point to mark a query or to express a doubt; do not follow indirect questions with a question mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "Who is this?" ; Indirect question: He asked whether he was ill. (no question mark)

rubrics_metrics.name: 130. Interrogation point placement with quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the question mark inside the quotation marks only when it is part of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The question: "Who is who, and what is what?" ; Were you ever in "Tsintsinnati"?

rubrics_metrics.name: 131. General uses of the colon
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon marks a discontinuity greater than a semicolon and less than a period; commonly used (i) to emphasize close connection between two clauses each of which is a complete sentence, (ii) to separate a grammatically complete clause from a following illustration or amplification, (iii) to introduce a formal statement, extract, or speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the material after the colon is a clause quoted in the middle of a sentence, use a comma before the quotation. Examples provided show usage in each of the three common functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 132. Colon replaces words like 'namely' or 'as follows' when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an implied 'namely' or similar phrase is used, follow with a colon if what follows consists of one or more grammatically complete clauses; otherwise use a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "This is true of only two nations ... in Europe: Great Britain and France" vs. "— viz., Great Britain and France." Also examples contrasting colon vs. comma usage with 'for example' or 'for instance'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 133. Use colon after salutatory phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a colon after the salutatory phrase at the beginning of a letter and after the introductory remark of a speaker addressing the chairman or audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "My dear Mr. Brown:" ; "Mr. Chairman, Ladies and Gentlemen:"

rubrics_metrics.name: 134. Colon in scripture and time notations
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a colon between chapter and verse in Scripture passages and between hours and minutes in time indications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Matt. 2:5-13; 4:30 P.M.

rubrics_metrics.name: 135. Colon between place of publication and publisher
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a colon to separate the place of publication and the publisher's name in literary and bibliographical references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Clement of Alexandria (London: Macmillan).

rubrics_metrics.name: 136. Colon placed outside quotation marks unless part of quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the colon outside quotation marks, unless it is part of the quoted material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrating when colon belongs inside vs. outside following quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 137. Semicolon to mark divisions stronger than a comma
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a semicolon to mark the division of a sentence somewhat more independent than that marked by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show semicolons joining parallel clauses or balancing contrasted clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: 138. Semicolon in complex enumerations
rubrics_metrics.description: In enumerations, use a semicolon between different items if they consist of more than a few words, especially if individual clauses contain internal punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include lists of countries with parenthetical comments and enumerated legal/justification items.

rubrics_metrics.name: 139. Semicolon in Scripture references
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a semicolon to separate Scripture passages that contain chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: 140. Semicolon placement relative to quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the semicolon outside the quotation marks unless it is part of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard punctuation placement rule; examples accompany text.

rubrics_metrics.name: 141. General use of the comma
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the comma to indicate the smallest interruptions in continuity of thought or grammatical construction that contribute to clearness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous illustrative examples show commas clarifying apposition, restrictive vs. nonrestrictive clauses, and lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: 142. Comma to separate proper nouns of different individuals/places
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate proper nouns belonging to different individuals or places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "To John, Smith was always kind"; "To America, Europe awards the prize of mechanical skill."

rubrics_metrics.name: 143. Serial (Oxford) comma guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma before 'and', 'or', and 'nor' connecting the last two links in a sequence of three or more, or where links are lengthy or complex; always put a comma before 'etc.'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tom, Dick, and Harry; either copper, silver, or gold. But omit when links form a brief tight phrase: "a man good and noble and true".

rubrics_metrics.name: 144. Commas around clauses introduced by conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily put a comma before and after clauses introduced by conjunctions like 'and', 'but', 'if', 'while', 'as', 'whereas', 'since', 'because', 'when', 'after', 'although' etc., especially if the subject changes; but omit when the preceding clause is not logically complete without them, or in brief close-welded phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed examples show when commas are appropriate or should be omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: 145. Use comma after introductory conjunctive adverbs/phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Words or phrases such as 'now', 'then', 'however', 'indeed', 'therefore', 'moreover', etc., should be followed by a comma when at the beginning of a sentence or clause; they should be set off by commas when inserted mid-sentence to mark a distinct break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also lists exceptions (no comma when connection is close or when adverb follows verb) with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: 146. Omit comma before 'rather' in certain expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferably omit the comma before 'rather' in expressions like 'measured in this way rather than by...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "The time-value is to be measured in this way rather than by the time-equivalent of the strata."

rubrics_metrics.name: 147. Comma between adjectives when last is more directly related
rubrics_metrics.description: If among several adjectives preceding a noun the last bears a more direct relation to the noun than the others, do not place a comma before that last adjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the admirable political institutions of the country' vs. 'a handsome, wealthy young man.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 148. Set off participial clauses with commas
rubrics_metrics.description: Participial clauses, especially those that contain explanations of the main clause, should usually be set off by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Being asleep, he did not hear him'; 'Exhausted by a hard day's work, he slept like a stone.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 149. Comma before 'not' introducing antithetical clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma before 'not' when it introduces an antithetical clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Men addict themselves to inferior pleasures, not because they deliberately prefer them, but because ...'

rubrics_metrics.name: 150. Use commas for parenthetical/adverbial/appositional clauses; use dashes for more disconnected insertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use commas to indicate parenthetical, adverbial, or appositional clauses or phrases that are structurally disconnected but logically integral; use dashes to indicate clauses both structurally and logically disconnected; never use both together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples contrasting comma use with dash use and illustrating prohibition of combining them.

rubrics_metrics.name: 151. Comma to separate identical or closely similar words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate two identical or closely similar words even if grammar does not require it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Whatever is, is good'; 'What he was, is not known.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 152. Commas around complementary/qualifying adjectival phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: In adjectival phrases, a complementary, qualifying, delimiting, or antithetical adjective added to the main epithet preceding a noun should be preceded and followed by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This harsh, though perfectly logical, conclusion'; 'The most sensitive, if not the most elusive, part ...'

rubrics_metrics.name: 153. Commas to separate coordinate clauses ending in a governing word
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more coordinate clauses ending in a word governing or modifying another word in a following clause should be separated by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrating such constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 154. Comma to separate two numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate two numbers in running text (e.g., 'In 1905, 347 teachers attended the convention').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also used in date expressions like 'November 1, 1905'. (See related rule 160.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 155. Comma to indicate omission of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to indicate the omission, for brevity or convenience, of a word or words whose repetition is not essential to meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'In Illinois there are seventeen such institutions; in Ohio, twenty-two.' Often such constructions may be smooth enough not to call for commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: 156. Comma before brief direct quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: A brief direct quotation, maxim, or similar expression should be separated from the preceding part of the sentence by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'God said, Let there be light.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 157. Comma before 'of' with residence or position
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma before 'of' in connection with residence or position (e.g., 'Mr. and Mrs. McIntyre, of Detroit, Mich.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions when the place-name has become part of the person's name (e.g., 'Clement of Alexandria').

rubrics_metrics.name: 158. Use en-dash, not comma, between consecutive pages in references
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a comma between consecutive pages in literary references; use an en-dash (exception: scriptural references may differ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: pp. 4, 7-8, 10; Ezra 5:7-8 (or Ezra 5:7, 8).

rubrics_metrics.name: 159. Comma after digits indicating thousands
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma after digits indicating thousands, except when used as a date or in a page-reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1,276; 10,419; January, 1909; p. 2461. Note: some journals (Astrophysical Journal, Botanical Gazette) do not use comma with four figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: 160. Separate month and year with a comma
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate month and year (and similar time divisions) by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: November, 1905; New Year's Day, 1906. Note: some journals do not use this comma.

rubrics_metrics.name: 161. Omit comma in signatures and article openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the comma in signatures and at the beginning of articles after the author's name followed by address, title, or position in a separate line, or after an address followed by a date line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show author name on its own line followed immediately by position/address without comma.

rubrics_metrics.name: 162. Comma placement with quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is always placed inside the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard rule; examples throughout punctuation section show this practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 163. Apostrophe marks omitted letters or figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an apostrophe to mark the omission of letters in contractions or of figures in dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ne'er, don't, 'twas, 'takin' me 'at'; m'fg; the class of '96.

rubrics_metrics.name: 164. Forming the possessive with apostrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the possessive case of nouns, common and proper, by adding an apostrophe, or apostrophe + s as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a man's, horses' tails; Scott's Ivanhoe, Jones's farms.

rubrics_metrics.name: 165. Apostrophe in plurals of numerals and rare coinages; possessives of proper names ending with sibilant
rubrics_metrics.description: Form plurals of numerals and rare/novel coinages with apostrophe + s; for proper nouns of more than one syllable ending in a sibilant add apostrophe alone, monosyllabic names add 's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in the 1900's; the Y.M.C.A.'s; 'the Tommy Atkins' of England' (but: the Rosses).

rubrics_metrics.name: 166. Dash denotes sudden break or transition
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash denotes a sudden break, stop, or transition in a sentence, an abrupt change in construction, a long or significant pause, or an unexpected/epigrammatic turn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Do we — can we — send out educated boys and girls ...?' ; 'To be or not to be — that is the question.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 167. Use dashes for parenthetical clauses that are both logically and structurally independent
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer dashes (rarely parentheses) for parenthetical clauses that are both logically and structurally independent interpolations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show using dashes when the parenthesis is emphatic or structurally separate.

rubrics_metrics.name: 168. Use dash to introduce emphatic or explanatory clause repeating a phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a clause that lends emphasis to or explains/expands a preceding word or phrase (often repeating it) with a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'To him they are more important as the sources for history — the history of events and ideas'; 'Here we are face to face with a new and difficult problem — new and difficult, that is ...'

rubrics_metrics.name: 169. Use a dash where 'namely' is implied before parenthetical clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a 'namely' is implied before a parenthetical or complementary clause, a dash should preferably be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'These discoveries — gunpowder, printing-press, compass, and telescope — were the weapons ...'

rubrics_metrics.name: 170. Use dash before final summarizing clause
rubrics_metrics.description: In sentences broken into clauses, the final summarizing clause should be preceded by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example demonstrates a series of clauses followed by a dash then a summarizing clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: 171. Dash after a word/phrase set in separate line and succeeded by paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: A word or phrase set on its own line and succeeded by paragraphs (each implying the preceding heading) should be followed by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I recommend —' followed by itemized paragraphs beginning '1. That we kill him.' etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 172. Dash usage with side-heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a dash in connection with side-heads, whether 'run in' or paragraphed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show use in topical headings and side-headings.

rubrics_metrics.name: 173. Use dash (en- or em-dash) in place of 'to' for ranges and rules for numeric shortening
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a dash instead of the word 'to' when connecting two words or numbers (e.g., ranges). Use en-dash for month ranges and page ranges, em-dash for other uses; when connecting consecutive numbers omit hundreds from the second number unless the first ends in two ciphers; repeat hundreds in B.C. dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: May–July, 1906 (en-dash); May 1, 1905 — November 1, 1906 (em-dash); pp. 3-7 (en-dash); 1880-95, pp. 113-16; 387-324 B.C. (repeat hundreds). Note journal exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 174. Precede references with dash after independent quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a dash precede the reference (author, title, or both) following a direct quotation that consists of at least one complete sentence in footnotes or when cited independently in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I felt an emotion of the moral sublime ...' — Thirty Years, 1, 379.

rubrics_metrics.name: 175. Do not use dash with other punctuation except period
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash should not ordinarily be used in connection with any other point except a period; avoid constructions like 'Dear Sir: — I have ...' or pairing commas with dashes around a clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of correct and incorrect pairings are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: 176. Parentheses for enumerated divisions within text
rubrics_metrics.description: Place figures or letters used to mark divisions in enumerations run into the text between parentheses (e.g., (1) (2) (3)), and follow a specified scheme of notation and indentation for hierarchical lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides hierarchical scheme: A. I. 1. a) (i) (a) etc., and guidance on punctuation (periods with figures/capitals, parentheses with lower-case italic letters when paragraphed).

rubrics_metrics.name: 177. Limit parentheses for parenthetical clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Parentheses should not ordinarily be used for parenthetical clauses unless confusion would arise from using less distinctive marks, or unless the content is wholly irrelevant to the main argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show when parentheses are acceptable for interpolations or explanatory asides.

rubrics_metrics.name: 178. Brackets uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use brackets to enclose an explanation or note; to indicate an interpolation in a quotation; to rectify a mistake; to supply an omission; and for parentheses within parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate each use: editorial notes, interpolations, rectifying errors in quoted names, supplying omitted info in citations, and nested parenthetical usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: 179. Brackets for 'To be continued' notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like '[Continued from p. ...]' and '[To be concluded]' at ends and beginnings of articles/chapters should be placed between brackets, centered, set in italics, and in reduced type size per reduction rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layout guidance for continuation notices in periodicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: 180. Ellipses indicate omission or lacunae with format rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses indicate omission from a quotation of one or more words not essential to the idea, or illegible words/mutilations/lacunae. For an ellipsis at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence, four periods separated by a space (en-quad) should ordinarily be used, except in very narrow measures. If the preceding line ends in a point, do not include it in the four. For omitted paragraphs or lines in poetry, insert a full line of periods separated by em- or 2-em quads according to line length; periods should not extend beyond the longest type-line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples demonstrate mid-sentence ellipses, omitted lines, and poetry omissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 181. Treat ellipsis as part of citation and enclose in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipsis is part of the citation and should be enclosed within the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to bracket/quotation rules (see 178[3]).

rubrics_metrics.name: 182. Hyphen at line breaks and in many compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a hyphen at the end of a line that terminates with a syllable carried to the next line; use hyphens between many compound words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See subsequent numbered rules for detailed hyphenation patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: 183. Hyphenate compound adjectives before a noun
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate two or more words (except proper names forming a unity) combined into one adjective preceding a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: well-known author, first-class investment, better-trained teachers, nineteenth-century progress. When set in capitals or when a component contains more than one word, use an en-dash (e.g., FRANCO-PRUSSIAN WAR). Do not hyphenate adverbs ending in '-ly' or combinations following the noun.

rubrics_metrics.name: 184. Hyphenate nouns formed by two nouns in objective relation
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, hyphenate nouns formed by combining two nouns in an objective relation (one component derived from a transitive verb).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mind-leader, story-teller, office-holder; exceptions include short common compounds like lawgiver, taxpayer, proofreader, bookkeeper.

rubrics_metrics.name: 185. Hyphenate present-participle + noun formations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a present participle united with a noun forms a new noun with a meaning different from the separate words, or when a participle + preposition used absolutely forms a noun, use a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: boarding-house, dining-hall, sleeping-room, walking-stick, starting-point, working-man.

rubrics_metrics.name: 186. Hyphenation rules for compounds with book/house/mill/room/shop/work
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'book', 'house', 'mill', 'room', 'shop', and 'work' are printed as one word when the prefixed noun has only one syllable; hyphenated when it contains two; printed as two separate words when it contains three or more (general rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: handbook, schoolbook; pocket-book, story-book; boathouse, engine-house; handmill, handmill vs. water-mill; bedroom, lecture-room; tinshop, tailor-shop; metal-work (exceptions noted). Exceptions for appearance/statistical considerations (source-book, wheat-mill, school work).

rubrics_metrics.name: 187. Hyphenate compounds of 'maker', 'dealer', occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'maker', 'dealer', and words denoting occupation should ordinarily be hyphenated; likewise nouns denoting different occupations of the same individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: harness-maker, book-dealer, job-printer; soldier-statesman, poet-artist Rossetti. Exceptions: brief common words like bookmaker, dressmaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: 188. Hyphenation of compounds of 'store'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'store' should be hyphenated when the prefix contains only one syllable; otherwise printed as two words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: drug-store, feed-store (but: bookstore); grocery store, dry-goods store.

rubrics_metrics.name: 189. Hyphenate compounds of 'fellow'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'fellow' are always hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fellow-man, fellow-beings, play-fellow.

rubrics_metrics.name: 190. Hyphenate kinship compound words
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'father', 'mother', 'brother', 'sister', 'daughter', 'parent', and 'foster' should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: father-love (but fatherland), mother-tongue, brother-officer, foster-son.

rubrics_metrics.name: 191. Hyphenate 'great-' compounds indicating degree of descent
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'great' indicating the fourth degree in a direct line of descent (e.g., great-grandfather) require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: great-grandfather, great-grandson.

rubrics_metrics.name: 192. Hyphenate compounds of 'life' and 'world'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'life' and 'world' require a hyphen (e.g., life-history), with noted exceptions (e.g., lifetime).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: life-history, life-principle (but: lifetime), world-power.

rubrics_metrics.name: 193. Hyphenation rules for 'skin' compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'skin' with words of one syllable are printed as one word; with words of more than one syllable, print as two separate words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: calfskin, sheepskin; alligator skin.

rubrics_metrics.name: 194. Hyphenate compounds of 'master'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds using 'master' should be hyphenated, except for some fixed exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: master-builder, master-stroke (exception: masterpiece).

rubrics_metrics.name: 195. Hyphenate compounds of 'god'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds with 'god' are hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sun-god, rain-god.

rubrics_metrics.name: 196. Hyphenate 'half', 'quarter' etc. combined with a noun
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'half', 'quarter', etc. are combined with a noun they should be followed by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: half-truth, half-tone, quarter-mile, half-title.

rubrics_metrics.name: 197. Hyphenation for prefixes 'semi', 'demi', 'bi', 'tri', etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefixes like 'semi', 'demi', 'bi', 'tri' do not ordinarily take a hyphen; exceptions include long or unusual formations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: semiannual, demigod, biweekly, trimonthly; exceptions: semi-centennial, demi-relievo.

rubrics_metrics.name: 198. Hyphenate compounds of 'self-'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds beginning with 'self' are hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: self-evident, self-respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: 199. Hyphenation for 'fold' combinations depends on syllable count
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations with 'fold' are printed as one word if the number is one syllable; if the number has more than one syllable, print as two words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: twofold, tenfold; fifteen fold, a hundred fold.

rubrics_metrics.name: 200. Hyphenation for adjectives formed with '-like'
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives formed by suffixing 'like' to a noun are usually one word if the noun has one syllable (except when ending in w), but hyphenated if the noun has more than one syllable or is a proper noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: childlike, homelike, eel-like, American-like (but: Christlike).

rubrics_metrics.name: 201. Hyphenate title-parts like 'vice-', 'ex-', 'elect', 'general', 'lieutenant' connected to chief noun
rubrics_metrics.description: Words such as 'Vice-', 'ex-', 'elect', 'general', and 'lieutenant' as parts of titles should be connected to the chief noun by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vice-Consul Taylor, ex-President Cleveland, the governor-elect, the postmaster-general, a lieutenant-colonel.

rubrics_metrics.name: 202. Hyphenate compounds with 'by-'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds beginning with 'by-' should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: by-product, by-laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: 203. Hyphenation rules for prefixes co-, pre-, re-
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefixes 'co-', 'pre-', and 're-' take a hyphen when followed by the same vowel as that in which they terminate (co-operation, pre-empted, re-enter); generally they do not when followed by a different vowel or by a consonant (coequal, prearranged, reinstal). Exceptions include combinations with proper names, long/unusual formations, or cases where omission would change meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: co-operation vs. coequal; pre-Raphaelite, re-cover (cover again) vs. reformation (different meaning). Note: some journals print cooperate, reenter.

rubrics_metrics.name: 204. Omit hyphen in certain common compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the hyphen in words such as 'today', 'tomorrow', 'tonight', 'viewpoint', 'standpoint'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to other rules for related compounds (see 119).

rubrics_metrics.name: 205. Hyphenation for negative particles 'un-', 'in-', 'a-' and 'non-'
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative particles 'un-', 'in-', and 'a-' do not usually require a hyphen; 'non-' ordinarily calls for a hyphen except in the commonest words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: unmanly, undemocratic, inanimate; non-aesthetic, non-subservient; exceptions: nonage, nondescript, nonessential.

rubrics_metrics.name: 206. Hyphenate 'quasi-' prefix
rubrics_metrics.description: The prefix 'quasi' prefixed to a noun or adjective requires a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: quasi-corporation, quasi-historical.

rubrics_metrics.name: 207. 'Over-' and 'under-' prefixes usually closed
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefixes 'over' and 'under' when prefixed to a word should not usually be followed by a hyphen, except in rare cases (lengthy or unusual words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: overbold, overemphasize, underfed, undersecretary; exceptions: over-soul, under-man.

rubrics_metrics.name: 208. Latin prepositional prefixes normally closed
rubrics_metrics.description: Latin prepositions 'ante', 'anti', 'inter', 'intra', 'post', 'sub', 'super' when prefixed to a word do not ordinarily require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: antedate, antechamber, international, intramural, postscript; exceptions: ante-bellum, ante-Nicene, anti-Semitic, inter-university.

rubrics_metrics.name: 209. Hyphenate 'extra', 'infra', 'supra', 'ultra' prefixes generally
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Extra', 'infra', 'supra', and 'ultra' as a rule call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: extra-hazardous, infra-mundane, supra-temporal, ultra-conservative (but: Ultramontane).

rubrics_metrics.name: 210. Hyphenation in spelled-out fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: In spelled-out fractional numbers, connect numerator and denominator with a hyphen unless either already contains a hyphen; however, do not hyphenate when common phrase forms are used (e.g., 'one half').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The year is two-thirds gone'; four and five-sevenths; but: 'One half of his fortune ...'

rubrics_metrics.name: 211. Use hyphen to indicate omitted common element in series of compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple compound words share a common component that is omitted from all but the last, indicate the omission with a hyphen (e.g., 'English- and German-speaking').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'one-, five-, and ten-cent pieces'; note that some consider this hyphen a Teutonism and object to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: 212. Hyphen indicates prefix or suffix as particle/syllable
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a hyphen to indicate a prefix or suffix when it is treated as a particle or syllable not complete in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The prefix a-'; 'The German diminutive suffixes -chen and -lein.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 213. Hyphen used to indicate syllabification
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ hyphens to indicate the syllables of a word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: di-a-gram, pho-tog-ra-phy.

rubrics_metrics.name: 214. Prescribed list of everyday hyphenated words
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of common everyday words that should be hyphenated regardless of other rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from list: after-years, cross-section, man-of-war, son-in-law, bas-relief, death-rate, page-proof, thought-process, title-page, post-office, wave-length, common-sense, fountain-head.
